question: You are given €10 and a stranger gets nothing. You may give them any part of it, and they cannot reply. How much?
answer: On average people gave away about 28%, though nobody could punish them. Part of that is being seen to be fair: in a later study, many players paid to slip out of the game before the stranger even learnt it existed. Engel pooled over 600 versions of the game to find the average.
move: Ask whether you would act the same if nobody could ever find out.
ask: When nobody is watching, what do I give, and what do I keep?

options.label: Nothing
options.mirror: Like 36% of players. The money came to you by chance, and keeping it broke no promise.

options.label: Something, under €5
options.mirror: Like about 4 in 10, the most common answer: a gesture to the stranger, not half your luck.

options.label: Half: €5
options.mirror: Like 17%. An even split felt fair to you, though nobody could see or punish you.

options.label: More than half
options.mirror: Like about 6%, most of whom gave it all. Their need felt bigger than your claim.

scene.why: Nobody can punish you here, yet most give something: fairness is felt, not only enforced.

source: Engel, Experimental Economics, 2011; Dana et al., 2006
reference: Engel, Dictator games: a meta study, Experimental Economics 14 (2011): 583-610; Dana, Cain & Dawes, What you don't know won't hurt me, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 100 (2006): 193-201
